text: A session token has exactly one job: being unguessable. This lesson covers authentication failures, A07:2025 in the current OWASP Top 10 — predictable tokens, sessions that outlive a logout, and password reset flows that quietly hand over an account. Each one is tested the same way the rest of this chapter has worked: inside a signed, authorized scope, never against a system you haven't been given explicit permission to touch.

If a token is a sequential integer, a timestamp, or a hash of the username, an attacker doesn't need to steal it — they can predict it. A real test captures several tokens issued back-to-back and looks for a pattern: is the value increasing on a fixed offset? And a token that merely looks random in base64 or hex still needs decoding, because that's often exactly where a timestamp or counter is hiding underneath.

Logout is one of the most commonly missed findings because it's invisible in normal use. The real test: capture the session token before logging out, log out, then replay that same token directly against an authenticated endpoint. If the server still honors it, the app only cleared the cookie client-side and never actually revoked the session in its own store. The same gap matters for password changes — every other active session for that account should be invalidated too, not just the one that changed it.

Password reset flows are a second, often weaker authentication path, and testers treat them that way. Three failures show up constantly: predictable reset tokens built from a timestamp or short numeric code, missing or excessive expiration that leaves an intercepted email usable for days, and user enumeration — where different response times or error text between a valid and invalid email let an attacker map every real account on the system.

A thorough test also checks whether a reset link is single-use and bound to the specific account it was issued for. A reset token that works against any account, not just the one it was emailed to, is a critical finding — it turns a convenience feature into a universal account-takeover path, and it's exactly the kind of flaw that gets missed when testing stops at 'does the reset email arrive.'

Entropy, server-side invalidation, and a tightly bound reset flow are what separate a secure authentication system from one that only looks secure in the browser. Next lesson, we move from the application's own login system to the APIs modern applications are increasingly built on — where the same authorization questions reappear as broken object-level authorization, mass assignment, and gaps in rate limiting.
